caps.t:
A guard at Alcatraz reached through the
bars to give a sleeping prisoner a push,

and the man's head rolled off
the bed and hit the floor.

It was soap and plaster
with real hair on top,

and the guards had been
counting it as a man all night.

Three prisoners were out on San Francisco
Bay on a raft made from more than 50
raincoats.
No body was ever found.
The FBI decided they'd died out there,

and then in 2013, the police got a
letter signed with one of their names.
So, did they actually survive?

Alcatraz was built to be the
prison nobody walked out of.

Al Capone did time there,
and so did Machine Gun Kelly,

and neither of them got off the
island until the government let them.
It sat on a rock in the middle of the bay,

at least a mile and a quarter
from the nearest shore.

The water around it
averages 50 to 55 degrees,

and the currents are strong enough to drag
a swimmer out under the Golden Gate and
into the Pacific.

In 29 years, 36 men tried
to get off the island,
and most of them were caught or shot dead.

Two drowned, and five more are still
listed as missing and presumed drowned.

Three of those five are
the men in this story.

Frank Morris was a career
criminal known for his brains,
and he'd broken out of a prison before.

John and Clarence Anglin were
brothers who'd grown up in Florida,

and they were in for robbing
a bank in Alabama at gunpoint.
A fourth prisoner, Allen West,
was in on the plan from the start.
Their cells were close together,

and the way out ran through
the back wall of each one.

All they had to dig with was
whatever they could scrounge.

At the back of every cell
was a small air vent,

and behind it was a narrow utility
corridor full of pipes that nobody watched.

The men started on the concrete around
those vents with old saw blades.
Then they built a drill.

The motor came out of a
broken vacuum cleaner,

which is a fairly bold
thing to run in a prison.
They worked at it night after night,

drilling rows of small holes close together
around each vent until the whole cover
could be lifted out.

In the daytime, they hid the holes behind
a suitcase or a piece of cardboard.
It took months, and in all that time,
not one guard noticed.

Now, a hole in the wall only
gets you into a corridor,

and a corridor still
leaves you on an island.

So they started on a boat, and they
built it on top of the cell block,
right over the guards' heads.

Inside the cell house, the top of their
cell block was a dark space under the roof
that the guards couldn't see into.

The men climbed up there through
the corridor and set up a workshop.

Over the following months, they
collected more than 50 raincoats,

some stolen and some picked
up around the prison.

They turned them into life vests
and a raft about 6 feet by 14,

big enough for three grown
men if nobody moved much.

To seal the seams, they pressed
them against the hot steam pipes,

and on Alcatraz, that's about as
close to a factory as you get.

For a pump, they turned a musical
instrument into a bellows.
They made paddles out of scraps of wood,
and they made the heads so that at night,

from the walkway, every bunk would
look like it had a man asleep in it.

The last job was the way out, a
ventilator in the roof above the workshop.
They worked it loose, and from below,
it still looked like it was bolted down.
By the second week of June 1962,
everything was ready.
Everything except Allen West's vent cover,
which was still in his wall.

On the evening of June 11th, Morris and the
Anglins pulled out their vent covers and
crawled into the corridor.

Allen West couldn't get his out because
he hadn't finished taking it apart.

By the time he got through,
the others were gone.

So the man who'd helped plan the whole
thing was still on the island the next

morning, and he's the one who
told the FBI how it was done.

The other three climbed
up to the workshop,
pushed out the roof ventilator,
and came out on top of the prison.

They crossed the roof and climbed down a
smokestack at the back of the cell house,
a stack about 45 feet high.

They got over the fence and down to
the northeast shore of the island,

and nobody saw them, which on Alcatraz
was supposed to be impossible.

There, they pumped up the raft
and pushed off into the dark.

What they couldn't do
anything about was the tide.

The water in the bay was
on the move that night,

and it would decide where
a small raft ended up.

Leave at the wrong time, and the
current takes you out to sea,
past the Golden Gate.

More than 50 years later, that tide is
still the best clue anyone has about where
they went.

The next morning, the guards counted
three heads that weren't real.
Before long, the FBI, the Coast Guard,

and the local police were
all out on the water.

Within two days, they'd found a packet
sealed in rubber with the Anglins' letters
and photographs inside.
A paddle turned up off Angel Island,
north of Alcatraz.

Then a life vest washed
up on Cronkhite Beach,
out past the Golden Gate.

That's the Pacific side, which is exactly
where you'd expect things to end up if the
current had swept the raft out to sea.
About six weeks after the escape,

the crew of a Norwegian freighter saw
what they said was a body floating in the
ocean beyond the bridge.
They didn't report it for months,
and it was never recovered.

Bits of rubber turned up too, but
they never found the raft itself,
and they never found the men.
The government says they drowned,
and it's got a strong case.

In water that cold, even a strong swimmer
can lose the use of his arms and legs

fast, and they were crossing
it at night on a homemade raft.

The currents around the
island had killed men before.
The Anglins' packet turned up in the bay,

and that's not something you'd
lose if your landing went well.

And not one of the three
has shown his face since,
not for certain anyway.

The FBI looked for 17 years, and it says
nothing credible ever turned up to show

they were alive, in
America or anywhere else.
These were career criminals.

Men like that usually get caught
doing the one thing they know,
and these three never were.

On December 31st, 1979,
the FBI closed its case.

It concluded they hadn't survived the
crossing and handed the file to the US
Marshals, who kept looking.

But the Anglin brothers' family
never believed any of it.

The family says their mother got Christmas
cards and roses for years after the
escape.

None of the envelopes they've
shown has a postmark though,

so nobody can say when
the cards were sent.

The handwriting was looked
at and called theirs,

but that only tells you
who wrote the cards,
not when.

In 2015, the family went further and
released a photo they said showed John and
Clarence on a farm in Brazil in 1975.
The photo came from a family friend,

and a forensic imaging expert said the faces
looked more like the brothers than not.

A retired marshal's deputy who worked the
case said the men in the photo weren't the

Anglins, and he called
the friend a con man.
Then there's the letter.

In 2013, the San Francisco Police
got a letter signed John Anglin.
It said he was 83, he had cancer,

and all three of them
had made it that night,
but only just.

It said Frank Morris died in
2008 and Clarence in 2011,
and it offered a deal.

If they announced on TV that he'd get
medical help and no more than a year in jail,

he'd write back and say
exactly where he was.
The FBI tested it for fingerprints,
DNA, and handwriting.
The results were inconclusive.

So the letter could be real, or it
could be somebody's idea of a joke,

and there's no way to
tell which from the paper.
That leaves the tide.

In 2014, scientists at Delft University in
the Netherlands ran a model of the bay's
currents for that exact night.

They set virtual rafts loose from Alcatraz
at different times and watched where they
went.

Leave too early, and the
tide carries you out to sea.

But leave between about 11:00
and midnight and paddle hard,

and you could land near the north
end of the Golden Gate Bridge.

And in that same run, the debris floated
back into the bay towards Angel Island,
which is where the paddle was found.

So that paddle off Angel Island looked
like one more sign they'd drowned.

But it fits a crossing that worked just
as well if they set off at the right time.
Nobody knows exactly when they did though.

The FBI's account only says
they left in the evening.
So, did they make it?
On the evidence, they probably didn't,

but it's a lot closer than the
official story makes it sound.
Nothing they left behind proves they died,

and the tide model shows
the crossing could be done.

The cards, the photo, and the letter
are the only signs that they made it,

and nobody has been able
to prove any of them.

And staying hidden for 60
years without one slip,

with the FBI and then the
marshals looking for you,
is a very hard thing to pull off.
If we had to bet, we'd say the bay won.

The marshals don't think
the bet's settled either.

In 2022, they put out computer images of
what the three might look like as old men,
and the case is still open.

In 2012, they said they'd keep hunting
the three until they're arrested,
proven dead, or reach the age of 99.

Frank Morris would have
turned 99 in September 2025.
John Anglin would reach it in 2029,
and Clarence in 2030.

By the marshals' own rule, that keeps
the two brothers wanted men until then.

Our next story is another American
landmark with an official number on it,
the 96 men who died building Hoover Dam,
and the deaths the count left out.
